explanations.explanation: Tenderly, friend. The words are “Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her…” Not a lecture, not a scolding, just a gentle voice. After years in the back of a junk drawer, I can tell you that gentle is the voice you want to hear.

I see why you'd guess it, because sometimes a message needs a deep voice. But this one starts with “Comfort, comfort My people,” and the instruction is to speak tenderly. Stern doesn't fit a message that begins with comfort. This is a soft-voice moment, friend.

No stiff speech and no clipboard here, friend. I picture someone in a tie reading a memo, and that's not the picture. The text says to speak tenderly to Jerusalem. That's warm, and it's the opposite of a form letter.

I get why you'd pick it, since a lot of heavy words are flying around in this verse. But the text says the opposite. Jerusalem is told that “her iniquity has been pardoned.” Pardoned means it's been dealt with, and nothing is left waiting.

False is right, friend. The text says her forced labor has been completed and “her iniquity has been pardoned.” Nothing is sitting on a shelf waiting for her. Pardoned means done, and this is good news from the start.

The wilderness is right. The voice says, “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness.” It's not a spot with a nice view or a gift shop. This is the open, empty stretch, and the work starts right there.

The temple courts sound like a natural place to get ready for the LORD. But the voice doesn't send anyone there. It says, “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness,” and the highway goes in the desert. The whole job happens out in the open.

Staying inside the walls sounds safe and comfortable. But that's not what the voice says. The way is prepared “in the wilderness,” and the highway is “in the desert.” This work happens outside the city, friend.
Lifted is right. The text says, “Every valley shall be lifted up.” The low spots come up so the road is ready. It's like filling the world's biggest pothole, and I'd pay to watch that crew.

Digging feels like road work, so I see why it came to mind. But a valley is already low, and the text says it shall be “lifted up.” Digging goes the other direction. This job is about bringing the low places up.

Broken sounds dramatic, friend, and it does have some action movie energy. But the verse never says the valleys are broken. It says every valley “shall be lifted up.” Nothing here gets smashed. It gets raised.

I see the thinking: valleys go up, so everything goes up. But the text sends the mountains the other way. It says every mountain and hill is “made low.” Valleys come up, and mountains and hills come down.
False is right, friend. The valleys are lifted up, but every mountain and hill is “made low.” High ones come down and low ones go up. That's how you end up with a smooth road.
The glory of the LORD is right. The voice says, “And the glory of the LORD will be revealed.” That's the whole reason for all that road work. It's a big reveal, and the road is only the opening act.

Treasure feels like a good guess, because a reveal makes you think of something buried. But the voice never mentions treasure. What's revealed is “the glory of the LORD.” That's better than any chest of gold.

A new building is a reasonable thing to expect when a road is being prepared. But the text doesn't say a word about a temple here. It says “the glory of the LORD will be revealed.” The reveal is about Him, not a building.

All humanity together is right. The text says, “all humanity together will see it.” Nobody is left out and nobody gets a private showing. Everybody sees it at the same time, like one giant crowd looking up at the same sky.

The elders are a common pick when something important happens. But the voice doesn't narrow it down to one group. It says “all humanity together will see it.” The whole human family is in the audience.

I see why priests came to mind, since they're close to holy things. But the text isn't saving this for a few people. It says, “all humanity together will see it.” That's everyone, friend, not just the ones near the temple.

explanations.answer: The grass withers and the flowers fall
explanations.explanation: That's right. When the breath of the LORD blows on them, “The grass withers and the flowers fall.” It's a blunt picture of how brief we are. I'll say it: I've seen my own edges go soft, and the picture fits.

explanations.answer: The grass grows and the flowers bloom
explanations.explanation: That would be a happier picture, and I'd love to bake with it. But the text goes the other way. When the breath of the LORD blows, “The grass withers and the flowers fall.” This verse is about how fragile people are.

explanations.answer: The grass bends and the flowers sway
explanations.explanation: Swaying sounds peaceful, like a nice breeze on a good day. But the verse is stronger than that. When the breath of the LORD blows on them, “The grass withers and the flowers fall.” They don't sway and bounce back, friend.
Forever is right. “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.” Everything else fades, but His word stays standing. That's the part to hold onto, friend.

Alone is an interesting guess, but the verse doesn't picture God's word that way. It says the word of our God “stands forever.” It's not about being by itself. It's about lasting when everything else fades.
Silent is a nice-sounding word, but it points the opposite way. The verse says the word of our God “stands forever.” A word that stands forever is still speaking. It doesn't go quiet.

Keeping quiet makes sense if you're nervous about a big message. But the herald gets different orders. Jerusalem is told, “Raise your voice loudly,” and then, “Lift it up, do not be afraid!” This is no whisper, friend.
False is right. The herald is told, “Raise your voice loudly, O Jerusalem, herald of good news.” Then comes “Lift it up, do not be afraid!” This message is meant to be heard, so don't hold it in.
That's right. The herald says to the cities of Judah, “Here is your God!” It's the whole message in four words. I think that's why it's worth shouting from a mountain.
News about walls would be good news, I'll give you that. But the herald isn't told to say anything about walls. The message is “Here is your God!” That one line is the whole announcement.

I see why you picked it, because that's a message people would cheer for. But the text never has the herald say it. The herald says to the cities of Judah, “Here is your God!” The big news is about who is arriving.

That's right. “The Lord GOD comes with might, and His arm establishes His rule.” His arm is how He sets up His rule, and that's strength with a purpose. Say it with me, friend, because that verse has weight.
Building is something arms do, so I see why it fits. But the verse doesn't mention a temple. It says, “His arm establishes His rule.” That's the job of His arm in this verse.
That's a mighty picture, and it makes sense for a mighty arm. But this verse says something else. “His arm establishes His rule.” Nothing here mentions the sea, friend.
Shepherd is right. “He tends His flock like a shepherd.” The One who comes with might is also the One who tends. That's a surprising pair, and it's all in the same short stretch of verses.

A gardener tends things too, so I get why you picked it. But the verse names a flock, and a flock goes with a shepherd. The text says, “He tends His flock like a shepherd.” I'd only trust myself with a rolling pin, and I'm not much of a gardener either.
A potter works with careful hands, so it's a fair guess. But the verse says, “He tends His flock like a shepherd.” A flock needs a shepherd, not a potter. Different picture, friend.
Close to His heart is right. The verse says, “He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart.” The lambs aren't made to walk it alone. They get carried right up against Him.

Far fields sound like what a shepherd might do with sheep, so I see why you picked it. But the verse says something closer. He “carries them close to His heart.” The lambs are held near, not sent far.
A riverbank is a nice picture for a shepherd scene. But the text doesn't take the lambs there. He gathers them “in His arms and carries them close to His heart.” The place is close to His heart.
I see why you thought so, since some people picture a shepherd pushing the flock hard. But that's not this shepherd. The verse says, “He gently leads the nursing ewes.” Gently leads, not drives hard.
False is right. The verse says, “He gently leads the nursing ewes.” There's no hurrying them along. After all that might in verse 10, this is a soft side of the same Lord GOD.
